source_title: Are youth worried they will be worse off than their parents?

A protester holds a placard reading "scorned youth" during a demonstration by high school and university students, supported by teachers' union and school parents, in Paris on October 6, 2026 as part of a nationwide day of demonstrations and blockades, voicing anger over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated school buildings, which students blame on years of underinvestment. | Photo Credit: Reuters
Europe is seeing a wave of protests against economic inequalities and poor living standards. The immediate causes vary across countries, from the housing crisis in Spain and issues with the education system in France to public anger over perceived corruption in Serbia and Albania. But one thing is common: youth at the vanguard. Europe always had space for democratic dissent and has seen major protests to influence state systems and public policy. But with more and more youth taking the streets across the continent and beyond, are these protests merely reactionary, or is there a generational, existential anxiety at play? Are youth worried they will be worse off than their parents? Gilles Verniers and Rohit Azad discuss in a conversation moderated by Vighnesh P. Venkitesh .
